title: The Correspondence of a Single Thought
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: Excerpted from Master Chewu's Posthumous Collection: Letter in Reply to the Layman Xiangyan

inline.s: Excerpted from Master Chewu's Posthumous Collection
Letter in Reply to the Layman Xiangyan

[You must deeply believe and truly comprehend: outside the mind there is no Buddha, and outside the Buddha there is no mind; the whole mind is the Buddha, and the whole Buddha is the mind. When a single thought comes to the fore, there is the correspondence of a single thought; when every thought comes to the fore, there is the correspondence of every thought.]

One should deeply believe and truly comprehend the state of 'outside the mind there is no Buddha, and outside the Buddha there is no mind; the whole mind is the Buddha, and the whole Buddha is the mind' — wherein only this single thought of Buddha-recitation remains, and no other thought. When one's practice reaches this state, then: when one thought (a pure, unadulterated thought of Buddha-recitation) comes to the fore, there is the correspondence of one thought; when every thought comes to the fore, there is the correspondence of every thought.
Here, 'mind' refers to the mental thought; 'Buddha' refers to the Buddha's name being recited; 'correspondence' means 'this mind makes the Buddha, and this mind is the Buddha.' Master Chewu said:
“With one thought corresponding, one thought is the Buddha; with every thought corresponding, every thought is the Buddha.”
On Buddha-Recitation (Recorded Teachings of Master Chewu)

[Outside the mind there is no Buddha, outside the Buddha there is no mind; the whole mind is the Buddha, the whole Buddha is the mind] Outside the mental thought there is no Buddha-thought (the thought of Buddha-recitation), and outside the Buddha-thought there is no mental thought; the whole mental thought is the Buddha-thought, and the whole Buddha-thought is the mental thought. This describes the state in which the mental thought and the Buddha-thought completely coincide, and the thought of Buddha-recitation is pure and unadulterated.
Concerning this instruction of Master Chewu, Master Yinguang, in his Answers to the Questions of the Buddha-Recitation Layman (i.e., Zhou Mengyou), says:

“Question: Is the word 'thought' in 'a single thought comes to the fore' and 'every thought comes to the fore' the same in meaning as the word 'mind' in 'mind and Buddha'? Answer: Mind and thought are just one thing. Only, with regard to what is always present, it is called mind; with regard to what arises in the present, it is called thought. Question: Do the four phrases 'outside the mind there is no Buddha, and outside the Buddha there is no mind' refer to the virtue of the nature, and do the four phrases 'a single thought comes to the fore, a single thought corresponds' refer to the virtue of cultivation? Answer: Both refer to the virtue of cultivation, because 'outside the mind there is no Buddha, and outside the Buddha there is no mind' is brought about by practice. Question: The four phrases 'a single thought comes to the fore, and a single thought corresponds' — can a beginner attain this, or can only a long-time practitioner attain it? Answer: The beginner has the beginner's correspondence, and the long-time practitioner has the long-time practitioner's correspondence — how can one rigidly cling to it?”

[If you can only keep this thought constantly before you, that is the true sign of efficacy. To seek efficacy apart from this thought is to create interruption, to lose intimacy, and to enter a wrong path! The sutra says: 'This mind makes the Buddha, and this mind is the Buddha.' This is exactly what it means.]

As long as you keep this thought (the pure, unadulterated thought of Buddha-recitation) constantly before you, that is the true sign of efficacy. To seek efficacy apart from this thought is to create interruption, to lose intimacy, and to enter a wrong path! The sutra says:
“This mind makes the Buddha, and this mind is the Buddha.”
This is exactly the state it speaks of!
